content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 19, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health RSV Activity and Interference Shape Human Metapneumovirus Timing in US Study by November 17, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 RSV Activity and Interference Shape Human Metapneumovirus Timing in US Study Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Transmission rates of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) are shaped by viral interference from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) rather than regional climate conditions, according to an age-stratified dynamic transmission modeling study conducted by Ke Li and colleagues. HMPV causes acute lower respiratory infections that primarily affect young children and older adults, generating seasonal outbreaks that peak annually in March or April across the United States and other temperate regions in the Northern hemisphere. To determine the poorly understood drivers of this seasonality, the research team analyzed laboratory-confirmed HMPV cases alongside age-specific emergency department visits across ten distinct US regions. The researchers tested several candidate transmission models to evaluate whether environmental factors or viral interference governed observed spatiotemporal patterns. Dynamic models incorporating climate variables into the transmission rate, including vapor pressure, precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, and minimum temperature, could not capture the timing of HMPV activity across all ten regions. In contrast, the timing of HMPV outbreaks was consistently associated with RSV activity, demonstrating that the HMPV transmission rate is directly reduced in the presence of circulating RSV. This viral interference proved essential for explaining regional variations in infection cycles. Among the candidate models analyzed, only those incorporating an RSV-associated term successfully reproduced the biennial patterns of HMPV documented in certain regions. These multi-year cycles are characterized by alternating epidemic waves classified by the authors as “late-small” and “early-large” outbreaks, a dynamic that purely climate-driven formulations failed to replicate. Using the best-fit model containing the RSV-associated term, the investigators predicted how future RSV interventions might influence HMPV spread. Although RSV interventions reduce viral competition between the two pathogens, model forecasts indicate that such measures are unlikely to result in a substantial increase in HMPV activity. The authors concluded that defining these spatiotemporal dynamics and pathogen interactions will help inform future seasonal forecasting and intervention strategies for HMPV.
